title: The 50 Percent Problem
author: Build Cognitive Resonance
summary: This essay uses a newly viral study, 'The Generative AI Learning Penalty: Evidence from Chinese Secondary Education,' to argue that generative AI is causing large-scale, measurable harm to student learning, coining the term '50 Percent Problem' as a counterpart to the ed-tech field's older 'Five Percent Problem.' Drawing on data from roughly 27,000 Chinese students tracked from 2023 to mid-2025, the author shows that the roughly half of students who fully outsourced homework to AI spent less time studying and scored higher on homework, yet performed dramatically worse on closed-book monthly exams (a 20% average decline) and on China's high-stakes placement exams (up to 24% lower), while students who never used AI tracked identically to pre-AI baselines. The piece argues this constitutes rare, rigorous, real-world causal evidence — as opposed to the mostly low-quality research that has dominated ed-tech studies of AI to date — and rebuts several counterarguments, including the claim that 'using AI intelligently' erases the harm and the hope that newer, more capable AI tools will shrink the penalty over time. It closes by endorsing cognitive scientist Dan Willingham's litmus test: AI should never substitute for tasks whose whole point is the mental work of learning.
points: The underlying study found that between 2023 and 2025, roughly 80% of Chinese secondary students started using generative AI and about 50% engaged in 'full homework outsourcing,' essentially stopping independent homework entirely — the basis for the author's '50 Percent Problem' framing.

Students who used AI studied less (often 45 minutes or less, versus roughly an hour for non-users) yet scored higher on homework than even the most studious non-AI-using peers, while simultaneously scoring far lower on monthly closed-book exams — a 20% average decline (1.4 SD) that the author calls 'Deadweight Learning Loss' and says exceeds estimated US pandemic-era learning loss.

On China's high-stakes placement exams, students who had used generative AI for two or more years showed estimated negative effects of 24% (1.5 SD) on the high school entrance exam and 18% (1.3 SD) on the college entrance exam, with no evidence of any offsetting learning benefit from AI use.

The author rebuts the counterargument that 'controlling for study time' shows AI users perform equally well, noting that of nearly 27,000 students only a vanishing handful of AI users continued to study 75+ minutes, making this an unrepresentative sliver used to obscure the study's central finding.

The piece notes a telling asymmetry: Chinese AI companies disable their products entirely during high-stakes testing periods, while OpenAI actively promotes ChatGPT on U.S. college campuses during finals week — and closes by endorsing cognitive scientist Dan Willingham's litmus test that AI should never substitute for the mental work that is the actual point of an assignment.
quotes: Generative AI does not suffer from this problem. Uniquely perhaps in the history of ed-tech, AI has been broadly embraced by students worldwide.
Between 2023 and 2025, approximately 80 percent of all students started using generative AI, and approximately 50 percent of all students engaged in "full homework outsourcing.
What's more, there is no evidence, none, of any corresponding learning benefit arising from students using AI.
To restate, the Used AI students studied less yet scored better than their peers.
In this sense, AI fosters a mental masquerade, scores go up as actual learning goes down.
I've labeled this the Deadweight Learning Loss to underscore the volume of harm caused by the generative AI learning penalty.
This is the 50 percent problem. Generative AI is cognitive cancer and we are doing next to nothing to stop it from spreading.
Artificial Intelligence tools should not substitute for tasks wherein students would benefit from doing the mental work themselves. Only use AI for what you already know how to do.
A tool that should only be used once you already know something is not a learning tool.
